body:
> `NaN` as it happens, is considered an infinite value,

Oh, that's surprising, [unrestricted double](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#idl-unrestricted-double) does the distinction between "*finite, non-finite, and special "not a number" values (NaNs).*". I would never have thought it got encompassed by either "finite" or "infinite" in specs wordings.

It seems odd to me that “infinite” would be considered NaN-inclusive here. The word “non-finite” is usually used when the intention is to refer to Infinity, -Infinity, _and_ NaN together (because NaN is neither finite nor infinite). The fact that there is a NaN-specific case following the “infinite” case suggests “infinite” was meant to refer to only Infinity and -Infinity here. What led to the conclusion that “NaN as it happens, is considered an infinite value”?

In my reading, Firefox is behaving correctly.

[Edit: Chrome/Edge also behave correctly. They don’t throw, they print a console warning (which an agent is free to do as they see fit; non-behavioral feedback like that isn’t a spec level concern). Safari’s behavior is the bug.]

> What led to the conclusion that “NaN as it happens, is considered an infinite value”?

I don't have direct access to IEEE 754 as it seems to be behind a paywall (for some damn reason), so I can't double check to be sure, but all Browsers implement https://tc39.es/ecma262/#sec-isfinite-number and all of them have the same result when you run `isFinite(NaN)` which returns `false`. Which I (as well as JSDOMs implementation it seems) used to infer that the inverse thus is true.

Now as you point out `NaN` could be considered _neither_ finite or infinite, as it is such a special value, which makes the Spec even more confusing to follow. I would speculate that (just as JSDOM) Safari uses `isFinite` to implement the Spec, and this throws out `NaN`.

> In my reading, Firefox is behaving correctly.

I would agree, but I think the text of the Spec should still be clarified to make this more obvious.

Blinks behaviour is alright, although confusing to developers - throwing a warning that you can not do what is asked, but doing it anyway can hardly be described as "behaving correctly" in my view, but I agree that this is not a spec level concern.

If the spec was more clear, im sure they wouldn't throw the warning in the first place though.


I have updated the original post to sound less authoritative on the conclusion of `NaN` being `infinite`.

> I don't have direct access to IEEE 754 as it seems to be behind a paywall (for some damn reason)

It’s ridiculous that a purported “standard” can be paywalled, yes :) ... _[Searching with “pdf” in the query may open a door.]_

IEEE 754’s _isFinite(x)_ and _isInfinite(x)_ do indeed both evaluate to false for any _x_ for which its _isNaN(x)_ would evaluate to true.

> Blinks behaviour is alright, although confusing to developers [...] If the spec was more clear, im sure they wouldn't throw the warning in the first place though.

I agree it’s an odd message. The motivation is almost certainly due to believing it’s useful to provide developer feedback for `foo.valueAsNumber = otherValueThatCoercesToNaN` rather than `foo.valueAsNumber = NaN` in particular, though — I doubt it stemmed from confusion on the part of the implementors. The `unrestricted double` conversion is in the Web IDL bindings layer, so it’s unlikely that setter-specific steps would have enough context to distinguish “NaN that was input directly as NaN” from “NaN that was produced by ToNumber(input)” when choosing to print the message.

> [...] throwing a warning that you can not do what is asked, but doing it anyway can hardly be described as "behaving correctly" in my view, but I agree that this is not a spec level concern.

When I say “behaving” / “behavior”, I mean runtime-observable behavior specifically (because nothing else can be material to HTML / web standards in general), and a console warning (it’s not thrown) isn’t runtime-observable. It would make sense to open a Chromium/Blink issue for the message to make the case that the message is more misleading than helpful. (It’s also very odd that it says “parse” imo.)

I shall open various tickets for Safari & JSDOM (Not following spec) and Chromium (confusing warning) then.

Given the details about `NaN` the Spec is technically valid and thus doesn't _require_ fixing, but given the fact that 2 independent groups have implemented it incorrectly in the same way, I still personally think it would be best to clarify the text, ever so slightly. I think I would have made the same mistake Safari & JSDOM did, and assumed that `if (isFinite(num))` is the correct implementation of the first step, while it really needs to be `if(isFinite(num) || isNan(num))`.
